transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jared Kim (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Lena Ortiz (Cosmos Head of ML), Ravi Patel (Cosmos Platform), Sophia Nguyen (Cosmos CTO), Ben Torres (SRE), Anika Rao (Data Scientist)

Auto-generated summary: customer experiencing cache evictions and latency spikes for 10k+ token sessions; investigating prefix reuse causing low hit-rate.

[00:00] Jared: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros then we'll hand over to maya to walk the kv cache arch and then dig into your traces and failures.
[00:23] Lena: thanks, jared. short background: we run multi-turn agents with ~15k token contexts, frequently reusing system prompts and domain-specific prefixes. saw latency jump and some hallucinated repeats after ~8k tokens.
[00:35] Maya: okay got it. first, high-level: our kv cache stores key/value per layer for autoregressive decoding. eviction occurs when total cache size exceeds pool sizing or per-model memory limits; we page older layers to host/ssd depending on config. i'll sketch the heuristics we use.
[01:05] Ravi: when you say page to host, do you mean real SSD paging or host DRAM? we've got node-local NVMe and a compressed in-memory page store.
[01:20] Maya: good question - by default we page to host DRAM first, then to NVMe as a fallback if configured. in private deployments we can toggle pure in-memory vs nvme-backed paging. note: NVMe paging adds ~15-60ms per affected token depending on IO path and concurrency.
[01:45] Ben: that seems high. our median latency target is 120ms; any paging could kill p95.
[01:53] Maya: agreed. that's why we try to avoid aggressive paging by tuning eviction thresholds and prefix heuristics.

[02:10] [Slide ref: https://redwood.app/decks/kv-cache-deep-dive.pdf] Maya: slide two shows three eviction triggers we observed in the field: pool-level memory pressure (shared GPUs), per-session TTL expiry, and explicit prefix invalidation from model switches. the interaction of prefix reuse causes the cache keyspace to expand unexpectedly.
[02:40] Anika: can you explain prefix reuse? we often take user messages and prepend a per-tenant intro that changes slightly each request (timestamp, small nonce).
[02:52] Maya: that's the classic pattern that causes high churn - if the prefix content changes a little, it's a different cache key, so the old keys stay in cache until eviction and new keys start filling up space. small variation = large cardinality.
[03:10] Sophia: any suggestions? we've tried normalizing prefixes but worried about losing auditability.
[03:20] Maya: two approaches: normalize non-semantic parts (strip timestamps / nonce), or use stable prefix pinning for system prompts - a pin keeps that prefix's KV pinned in GPU memory and excluded from eviction until unpinned. pinning costs reserved memory so you trade off capacity.

[03:45] [00:04:00] Ravi: how does pinning interact with batching? if pinned prefixes are large, will we reduce batch sizes?
[03:55] Maya: pinned keys are kept per-pool; they don't change batching logic per se, but they reduce available KV budget for other sessions, which may reduce concurrency or force earlier paging for non-pinned sessions. it's a capacity tradeoff.

[04:20] Jared: can you outline the eviction LRU vs size-aware heuristics you use? customers often ask LRU but their workload benefits from frequency-aware eviction.
[04:34] Maya: our default is an adaptive hybrid: we weigh recency and estimated reuse frequency (small LFU component) and add a per-prefix weight (pin weight). we also observe access patterns per model and can tune the decay window - shorter decay for high throughput chatbots, longer for long-context retrieval.
[04:56] Lena: our traffic has lots of repeated retrieval prompts across tenants - would setting a longer decay help?
[05:05] Maya: yes, if those repeats are frequent and you have capacity. if repeats are rare and prefixes are varying, longer decay just holds stale keys. we'd want trace data to recommend optimal decay.

[05:30] [00:06:00] Ben: about eviction-induced token duplication - we see repeated text output when a user's state is evicted mid-run. can you explain root cause?
[05:42] Maya: sure. duplication often happens when the KV cache used during beam decoding or streaming gets partially evicted and then reloaded from host with slight timing mismatch. the decoder then loses access to recent KVs and regenerates tokens, or continuity markers mismatch. it's more common in streaming + heavy batching scenarios.
[06:03] Anika: so is this a bug or expected behavior under memory pressure?
[06:10] Maya: a bit of both - it's expected under tight memory without pinning, but we have mitigations: conservative prefetch for active sessions, atomic swap of paged segments, and a short local token-history buffer to reconcile small mismatches. some mitigations require runtime flags in private deployments.

[06:35] [00:07:00] Ravi: you mentioned prefetch; how aggressive is prefetching? naive prefetch could blow memory.
[06:44] Maya: we use a predictive prefetch based on recent token access patterns - if a session is actively decoding, we prefetch the next N layers for that session only. N is configurable (defaults to 8 layers) and bounded by pool budget. we also rate-limit prefetch IOPS to avoid NVMe storms.

[07:10] [00:08:00] Maya: paging policy: 1) keep active sessions in GPU memory when possible; 2) cold sessions age into host DRAM; 3) coldest sessions go to NVMe. paging thresholds are tunable by a numeric budget per pool (e.g., 90% keep-in-gpu threshold).
[07:28] Sophia: for private deployments, what's the recommended NVMe config? we have JBOD NVMe on our worker nodes.
[07:36] Maya: we recommend local NVMe per node with >= 4k IOPS sustained and using our writeback cache; avoid networked block devices for KV paging. also ensure kernel io_uring enabled; we saw large latency variance with older fio configs.

[07:55] [00:09:00] Ben: we use compressed host DRAM store - does Redwood support compressed pages?
[08:02] Maya: yes, in private mode we can enable compressed paging to host. it reduces footprint but increases CPU overhead; for high-throughput low-latency workloads you may prefer more DRAM or larger GPU pools instead.

[08:20] [00:10:00] Jared: let's talk about quantization - any interactions with KV cache that change eviction patterns?
[08:28] Maya: quantization primarily affects model size and runtime memory per layer, so it changes the total KV budget. lower-precision models have smaller per-layer KVs, which improves cache capacity but can increase compute latency slightly if dequantization steps are needed. in practice, quantization helps reduce eviction frequency because keys are smaller.

[08:55] Anika: do you have numbers? e.g., 8-bit vs 4-bit impact on KV size?
[09:00] Maya: roughly 4-bit quantization halves the KV memory vs 8-bit, so you roughly double the number of tokens you can keep before eviction, but there are tradeoffs for per-token compute. we'll share benchmark graphs.

[09:20] [00:11:00] Ravi: we captured a trace where eviction spikes at 14:32 UTC - attached log shows many small prefixes being created.
[09:33] Maya: (scanning) i see a lot of unique prefix hashes with only 1-2 hits. that's the churn problem. did you do prefix normalization?
[09:40] Ravi: partial - we normalize timestamps but users sometimes include ephemeral ids.
[09:45] Maya: that explains it. next step: produce a normalized-sample and an anonymized trace; we can run the benchmark harness to simulate eviction under your distribution.

[10:05] [00:12:00] Lena: what about multi-tenant pools? we want resource isolation - can one tenant's cache behavior evict another's critical prefixes?
[10:18] Maya: by default pools are shared; we offer reserved segments per-tenant for Dedicated and Private. segments are enforced by capacity quotas; heavy tenants can be throttled or placed on dedicated queues. pinning per-tenant prefixes is also an option.

[10:35] Jared: any automated alerts we can set for early warning before eviction starts to impact user experience?
[10:42] Maya: yes - Redwood Console has cache pressure metrics and token churn heatmaps, and we can set SLO alerts (e.g., when cache hit-rate drops < 65% or paging IOPS spike). we'll include recommended alert thresholds in the playbook.

[11:05] [00:13:00] Ben: question on logs - we need actionable logs for repro, but not PII. what log level do you need?
[11:14] Maya: sample logs: per-session KV footprint, prefix hash, last-access timestamp, and eviction reason. those can be redacted on your side (hashes instead of full text). a 48-hour window is usually enough.

[11:40] [00:14:00] Sophia: security question: if you enable NVMe paging, where are pages stored and how are they encrypted?
[11:48] Maya: in private deployments pages remain on customer NVMe; Redwood runtime supports dm-crypt/LUKS integration and can work with customer KMS for key rotation. for hosted services we use encrypted host volumes and SSE; we'll attach SOC2 encryption details.

[12:10] [00:15:00] Anika: earlier you mentioned prefix hashing - what hash function do you use, and can we override it?
[12:19] Maya: we use a non-cryptographic fast hash (xxhash) over normalized prefix content; customers can override with a custom normalization hook in Private deployments. override requires testing because collisions or changed distribution can harm hit-rate.

[12:45] [00:16:00] Ravi: during a repro we saw mid-session thrashing where pages were written to NVMe and immediately read back - seemed like a ping-pong. any reason?
[12:56] Maya: ping-pong typically means the working set is slightly above GPU capacity and our decay window is oscillating; the scheduler may evict, then prefetch for active session, then evict again due to another demand spike. We mitigate with a hysteresis window - hold pages pinned for a short time after eviction if access probability is high.

[13:25] [00:17:00] Maya: also, check batching settings - large variable-length batching can spike transient requirements. setting max-batch-size and adaptive batch timeouts can smooth peaks.

[13:45] [00:18:00] Lena: about deployment modes - is there a recommended mode for long-context retrieval-heavy workloads?
[13:53] Maya: Dedicated with reserved GPU pools plus prefix pinning and increased DRAM for host cache tends to be the sweet spot. For the most sensitive workloads, Private on-prem with NVMe and tuned io_uring gives best predictability.

[14:15] [00:19:00] Ravi: any quick config changes to try in the short term?
[14:20] Maya: yes - 1) increase keep-in-gpu threshold from 85% to 92% (if capacity allows), 2) enable prefix normalization to strip ephemeral fields, 3) pin the top-5 system prefixes per tenant, 4) enable compressed host pages if you have CPU headroom.

[14:45] [00:20:00] Jared: we'll send a change bundle of those flags and a sample helm values patch for private.

[15:00] [00:21:00] Anika: curious - do you see any model-architecture-dependent differences? e.g., MPT vs LLaMA-style KV shapes?
[15:10] Maya: yes - different attention implementations change KV packing; some architectures have larger per-layer KVs. we maintain per-model profiles and kernel selection; we'll share per-model KV size multipliers.

[15:35] [00:22:00] Sophia: for the POC, how long to run the benchmark to be confident?
[15:42] Maya: we'd run a 48-hour synthetic run using your trace to capture diurnal effects, plus a short stress test to exercise worst-case concurrency.

[16:00] [00:23:00] Ravi: ok we'll extract 48h traces and scrub them.

[16:12] [00:24:00] Maya: one more note on prefix reuse mitigation: if normalizing isn't possible, consider a two-tier keying: a coarse-grain prefix key for shared KVs plus a session-local delta that is kept off-GPU. that reduces GPU cache growth at the cost of a small recompute for the delta.

[16:40] Anika: that sounds promising. any impact on output determinism?
[16:47] Maya: should be minimal if delta recompute is consistent; it's more work in the codepath but buys huge savings in KV budget.

[17:05] [00:25:00] Jared: we've covered a lot. let's recap next steps.
[17:12] Lena: recap would be good.

Recap and next steps:
[17:20] Maya: action items - we'll run repro when we get traces; recommend config changes listed earlier; provide pinning and normalization docs.
[17:30] Jared: i'll send the KV deep-dive deck and the benchmark harness link: https://redwood.app/playbooks/kv-cache-playbook and the benchmark repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-bench (anonymized).
[17:45] Ravi: we'll share traces and infra details.
[17:50] Ben: we'll schedule the in-cluster repro session for week of 9/17.

[18:00] Sophia: thanks, this was very actionable.
[18:05] Jared: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with links and a proposed slot.
